scenes.headline: How FAST-LIO2 fuses a LiDAR and an IMU
scenes.sub: The filter, the tree, and four systems measured on two walks
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Tsuru! Here is the loop inside FAST-LIO2, and what happened when I ran it beside three newer systems.

steps.say: Between sweeps, every IMU sample pushes the state forward, and the pose after each one is kept.
Those poses move every point back to where the sensor was at the end of the sweep.
Each point finds its five nearest map points, fits a plane, and its distance to that plane is the residual.
The filter solves, re-matches at the new pose, and solves again, until the step is tiny.
Then the scan goes into the map.

scenes.title: The gain that makes it cheap

parts.say: Thousands of residual rows go in here, but they are summed into one small matrix.

parts.note: a 23 by 23 inverse, whatever the point count
parts.say: So the only inverse is twenty-three by twenty-three, the size of the state, however many points the scan had.

labels: Insert: each new point walks down to a leaf
One side now holds more than 0.6 of it
Flatten it, rebuild it from the medians
Box delete: one label kills a whole subtree
Over half dead: rebuild, and free the dead
params.array: flattened into an array, deleted points dropped

steps.say: The map lives in an incremental k-d tree. New points land on one side, and one branch keeps getting deeper.
Every node on the way back up checks itself. This subtree has more than sixty percent on one side.
So it is flattened into an array and rebuilt balanced from the medians. The rest of the tree never moves.
When the map window slides on, a box delete marks a whole subtree dead with one label.
Once more than half of a subtree is dead, the next rebuild drops those points for good.

steps.say: First, a walk round an Oxford quad. FAST-LIO2 tracks to seven point two centimetres over two hundred and eighty-three metres. Super-LIO, eight.
